triage.name: Normal pressure hydrocephalus
triage.reason: Classic triad of gait disturbance, cognitive decline and incontinence in an older adult; diagnosis by history, exam and imaging, with several dementia look-alikes.

demographics: Most common in older adults; incidence rises with age
Slightly more common in men in most series

risk_factors.text: Prior meningitis or other CNS infection
Prior traumatic brain injury or neurosurgery

comorbidities: Prior stroke or vascular brain injury

chief_complaints.text: My walking has gotten worse and I feel unsteady
My memory and thinking aren't what they used to be
I've been having accidents and can't hold my urine
My feet feel like they're stuck to the floor when I start walking

hpi.onset: Insidious, over weeks to months, without a clear single event
hpi.duration: Usually months to a year or more by the time it is evaluated
hpi.progression: Slowly progressive; gait difficulty usually appears first and is the most disabling, with cognitive slowing and urinary symptoms developing later
hpi.location: Generalized; gait and balance are the main problems
hpi.quality: Shuffling, wide-based, unsteady walking with small steps; difficulty turning and a sense of the feet sticking to the floor
hpi.severity: Mild at first, then moderate to severe as falls and dependence increase
hpi.timing: Constant and gradually worsening; worse when starting to walk or turning
relieving: Holding onto furniture or a person
pertinent_negatives: Abrupt onset with focal weakness or numbness
Early behavioral or personality change out of proportion to memory loss

argues_against: Abrupt focal neurologic deficit suggesting stroke
Resting tremor and rigidity suggesting Parkinson disease
Early prominent hallucinations suggesting Lewy body dementia
Prominent behavioral change suggesting frontotemporal dementia
Painful urination suggesting urinary tract infection
Arthritic or orthopedic cause of gait difficulty

atypical.how_it_differs: Symptoms are often attributed to normal aging or coexisting conditions; gait slowing and cognitive changes may be the only obvious findings, and incontinence may be dismissed as prostate or bladder problems.

Normal pressure hydrocephalus is essentially an adult condition; children with hydrocephalus usually present with headache, vomiting, enlarging head size or developmental delay rather than the classic triad.

general.mild: Alert and oriented, walks with a slightly wide-based, shuffling gait; may use a cane
general.moderate: Slowed thinking and speech; unsteady, magnetic gait with difficulty turning; needs assistance or a walker
general.severe: Markedly impaired gait with frequent falls, significant cognitive slowing, and incontinence; dependent for mobility
general.critical: Bedbound or unable to stand safely, severely confused, incontinent, at high risk of falls and aspiration

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to stand, walk a few steps, turn around, and walk back
findings.finding: Shuffling, wide-based, unsteady gait with small steps and difficulty turning; feet seem stuck to the floor

findings.maneuver: Observe initiation of walking from a seated or standing position
findings.finding: Magnetic gait with hesitation and feet appearing glued to the floor

findings.maneuver: Pull test: stand behind the patient and gently pull back on the shoulders
findings.finding: Impaired postural reflexes with retropulsion or tendency to fall backward

findings.maneuver: Perform a brief cognitive screen such as the Mini-Mental State Examination or Montreal Cognitive Assessment
findings.finding: Slowed processing, impaired attention and executive function, and memory difficulty

findings.maneuver: Observe speed of movement and ask the patient to perform rapid alternating movements
findings.finding: Slowed movement and thinking without true rigidity or resting tremor

findings.maneuver: Ask about urinary control and, when appropriate, inspect for wet clothing or pads
Ask about bowel control and perform a rectal exam if indicated
Test cranial nerves II through XII
Test strength in all four limbs
Observe the hands at rest and during movement
Passively move the limbs to assess tone
Test light touch, pinprick and vibration sensation
Assess neck stiffness and perform Brudzinski and Kernig maneuvers if meningitis is suspected
findings.finding: No neck stiffness or meningeal signs

labs.caveat: Ordered to exclude hypothyroidism as a reversible cause of gait slowing, cognitive decline and incontinence; a normal result supports normal pressure hydrocephalus.
Low B12 is a reversible cause of cognitive impairment and gait difficulty; a normal level supports normal pressure hydrocephalus.
Opening pressure is normal or in the high-normal range (roughly 10–24 cm H2O); pressures above this range suggest an alternative cause of hydrocephalus.
Normal cell count; pleocytosis points to meningitis or another inflammatory process rather than normal pressure hydrocephalus.
Normal protein; elevated protein suggests an alternative cause such as chronic meningitis.
Normal glucose; low glucose suggests infection or malignancy.

imaging.preferred_when: Initial evaluation when MRI is unavailable or contraindicated

findings.text: Ventriculomegaly out of proportion to cortical atrophy
Enlarged temporal horns of the lateral ventricles
Periventricular hypodensity suggesting transependymal CSF flow
Narrowing of the high convexity sulci
No mass lesion, hemorrhage or midline shift

imaging.preferred_when: Preferred initial study; best characterizes ventricular size and excludes other causes

findings.text: Ventriculomegaly with an Evan's index greater than 0.3
Disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid space hydrocephalus (DESH): tight high-convexity sulci with widened Sylvian fissures
Periventricular T2 hyperintensity from transependymal CSF flow
Enlarged temporal horns of the lateral ventricles
Aqueductal or fourth ventricular flow void on T2
No mass, infarct or other structural cause of hydrocephalus

imaging.preferred_when: Selected cases when the diagnosis remains uncertain after MRI and CSF testing

findings.text: Ventricular reflux of radiotracer with delayed or absent clearance over the cerebral convexities
Normal or near-normal tracer distribution (argues against normal pressure hydrocephalus)

initial.why: Confirms ventriculomegaly, looks for DESH and excludes mass, infarct or other structural causes of the triad
Alternative when MRI is unavailable or contraindicated
Excludes hypothyroidism as a reversible cause of gait and cognitive decline
Excludes B12 deficiency as a reversible cause of cognitive impairment and gait difficulty
Baseline blood count before lumbar puncture and to look for anemia or infection
Baseline electrolytes and renal function before lumbar puncture

initial.only_if: bleeding risk, anticoagulant use or planned large-volume tap

confirmatory.why: Lumbar puncture with opening pressure and CSF analysis; normal opening pressure with normal cell count, protein and glucose supports normal pressure hydrocephalus and excludes meningitis
Removing 30–50 mL of CSF and reassessing gait and cognition within hours; improvement supports shunt-responsive normal pressure hydrocephalus

supporting.why: Continuous CSF drainage over 1–3 days with serial gait and cognitive testing when the tap test is equivocal
supporting.only_if: tap test result is equivocal or negative but clinical suspicion remains high

supporting.why: Shows ventricular reflux and delayed convexity clearance in selected uncertain cases
supporting.only_if: diagnosis remains uncertain after MRI and CSF testing

supporting.why: Characterizes the pattern of cognitive impairment and provides a baseline before shunting

supporting.test: Gait and balance assessment (timed up-and-go, gait velocity)
supporting.why: Objective baseline and follow-up measure of the most treatable symptom

not_indicated.why: No role unless infection or inflammation is suspected
No role unless infection or inflammation is suspected
No role in chronic gait or cognitive decline
Not relevant in the typical older adult presentation; obtain only if pregnancy is possible before imaging or procedures

decision_points: Confirm ventriculomegaly on imaging before considering CSF testing
Exclude reversible causes (hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, depression, medication effects) before attributing the triad to normal pressure hydrocephalus
Opening pressure must be normal or high-normal; higher pressures suggest an alternative cause of hydrocephalus
A positive tap test or external lumbar drainage trial supports referral for shunt evaluation
Coagulopathy or anticoagulation must be corrected before lumbar puncture or large-volume drainage

criteria.name: Clinical triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus
criteria.summary: Gait disturbance is the core and usually earliest feature; cognitive slowing and urinary incontinence develop later. All three are not required for diagnosis, and the gait disorder is the most responsive to treatment.
items: Gait disturbance (shuffling, magnetic, wide-based, difficulty turning)
Cognitive impairment (slowed processing, attention and executive dysfunction)

criteria.name: Supportive imaging and CSF findings
criteria.summary: Ventriculomegaly out of proportion to cortical atrophy, often with DESH pattern on MRI, and a normal or high-normal CSF opening pressure with normal CSF composition.
items: Tight high-convexity sulci with widened Sylvian fissures (DESH)
Normal CSF opening pressure, cell count, protein and glucose

differential.name: Parkinson disease
differential.why_considered: Older adult with shuffling gait, slowed movement and cognitive slowing
differential.trigger: Resting tremor, rigidity or a clear response to levodopa

history: Resting tremor that improves with movement
Gait difficulty with festination and freezing rather than magnetic feet
Levodopa-responsive symptoms
Constipation, anosmia and REM sleep behavior disorder may precede motor symptoms
exam: Masked facies and reduced arm swing
imaging: Normal ventricular size for age; no DESH pattern
DaTscan shows reduced presynaptic dopamine transporter uptake

differential.name: Alzheimer disease
differential.why_considered: Progressive cognitive decline in an older adult
differential.trigger: Prominent early memory loss with relatively preserved gait

history: Early and prominent short-term memory loss
Gait is relatively preserved until late
Urinary incontinence appears late, if at all
exam: No magnetic or wide-based gait early on
labs: B12 and TSH normal, as in normal pressure hydrocephalus
imaging: Diffuse cortical atrophy with proportionate ventriculomegaly

differential.name: Vascular dementia
differential.why_considered: Stepwise cognitive decline and gait difficulty in an older adult with vascular risk factors

history: Stepwise deterioration after strokes
Focal neurologic symptoms
Vascular risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes and smoking
imaging: Multiple infarcts or extensive white matter disease

differential.name: Lewy body dementia
differential.why_considered: Cognitive decline with gait impairment and visual symptoms in an older adult

history: Visual hallucinations early in the course
Fluctuating cognition and alertness
REM sleep behavior disorder
Neuroleptic sensitivity
imaging: DaTscan shows reduced dopamine transporter uptake

differential.name: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy
differential.why_considered: Gait unsteadiness and urinary symptoms in an older adult

history: Neck pain and stiffness
Numbness or clumsiness in the hands
Urinary urgency or retention
exam: Upper motor neuron signs such as hyperreflexia and Babinski sign

differential.name: Hypothyroidism
differential.why_considered: Reversible cause of cognitive slowing, gait impairment and fatigue in an older adult

history: Cold intolerance, constipation and weight gain
Dry skin and hair loss
exam: Delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes
Bradycardia, hoarse voice and periorbital edema
labs: Elevated TSH with low free T4

differential.name: Vitamin B12 deficiency
differential.why_considered: Reversible cause of cognitive impairment and gait difficulty

history: Paresthesias and numbness in the feet
Vegetarian diet, malabsorption or metformin use
labs: Low serum B12 with elevated methylmalonic acid and homocysteine
imaging: Subacute combined degeneration changes in the dorsal columns on MRI

differential.name: Medication-induced parkinsonism
differential.why_considered: Gait slowing and cognitive dulling in an older adult taking multiple medications

history: Temporal link to starting dopamine-blocking or other culprit medications
Improvement after stopping the medication
imaging: Normal ventricular size and no DESH pattern

severity.mild: Intermittent unsteadiness and slightly slowed walking; subtle memory complaints; occasional urinary urgency without accidents; independent in daily activities
severity.moderate: Persistent magnetic or wide-based gait with difficulty turning and occasional falls; noticeable cognitive slowing and attention problems; urinary urgency and occasional incontinence; needs a cane or walker and some help with activities
severity.severe: Frequent falls or inability to walk without assistance; significant cognitive impairment affecting judgment and daily function; established urinary and sometimes fecal incontinence; dependent for mobility and self-care
severity.critical: Bedbound or unable to stand safely with severe confusion and incontinence; high risk of falls, aspiration, pressure ulcers and institutionalization

red_flags.finding: Abrupt onset of focal weakness, numbness or speech difficulty
red_flags.meaning: Suggests stroke or another acute structural lesion rather than normal pressure hydrocephalus

red_flags.finding: Severe headache, fever or neck stiffness
red_flags.meaning: Suggests meningitis, encephalitis or subarachnoid hemorrhage
Suggests raised intracranial pressure or an alternative cause of hydrocephalus

red_flags.finding: Rapid progression over days to weeks
red_flags.meaning: Suggests an alternative diagnosis such as tumor, abscess or rapidly progressive hydrocephalus

red_flags.finding: New focal neurologic deficit or seizure
red_flags.meaning: Requires urgent imaging to exclude mass, hemorrhage or infarct

complications.name: Shunt malfunction or infection after ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement
clues: Return of gait, cognitive or urinary symptoms after initial improvement

special_populations.differences: Most common presentation; symptoms are often attributed to normal aging or coexisting conditions, and the full triad may not be present. Comorbid vascular disease and polypharmacy complicate assessment.

Normal pressure hydrocephalus is essentially an adult condition; children with hydrocephalus usually present with headache, vomiting, enlarging head size or developmental delay rather than the classic triad.

key_questions.question: What has changed about the way you walk, and when did it start?
key_questions.looking_for: Insidious, slowly progressive shuffling, wide-based, unsteady gait with small steps and difficulty turning; feet feel stuck to the floor

key_questions.question: Which problem came first — the walking, the memory, or the bladder?
key_questions.looking_for: Gait difficulty usually appears first and is the most disabling; cognitive slowing and urinary symptoms develop later

key_questions.question: How has your memory and thinking changed?
key_questions.looking_for: Slowed processing, trouble concentrating, impaired attention and executive function rather than isolated early memory loss

key_questions.question: Have you had trouble holding your urine or accidents?
key_questions.looking_for: Urinary urgency, frequency and incontinence; sometimes fecal incontinence

key_questions.question: Have you fallen or come close to falling?
key_questions.looking_for: Falls and near-falls from unsteadiness and impaired postural reflexes

key_questions.question: Has this come on suddenly, or gradually over months?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual over weeks to months; abrupt onset suggests stroke or another acute lesion

key_questions.question: Have you had a head injury, brain bleed, meningitis, or brain surgery in the past?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior subarachnoid hemorrhage, meningitis or other CNS infection, traumatic brain injury or neurosurgery — all risk factors

key_questions.question: Have you had a stroke, or do you have high blood pressure, diabetes or heart disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Vascular risk factors and prior stroke, which raise the possibility of vascular dementia as a look-alike

key_questions.question: What medications are you taking, including anything for mood, sleep, nausea or allergies?
key_questions.looking_for: Dopamine-blocking or sedating medications that could cause parkinsonism or cognitive dulling

key_questions.question: Any fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, or new weakness, numbness or trouble speaking?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; any of these suggests meningitis, subarachnoid hemorrhage, stroke or raised intracranial pressure rather than normal pressure hydrocephalus

key_questions.question: Any tremor when your hands are resting, or trouble with your vision?
key_questions.looking_for: Resting tremor or visual hallucinations point toward Parkinson disease or Lewy body dementia instead

key_questions.question: Any burning with urination, blood in the urine, or flank pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests a urinary tract infection or obstruction as the cause of the bladder symptoms

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have dementia or a movement disorder?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of neurodegenerative disease, which would raise an alternative diagnosis

reasoning_points: Older adult with the classic triad of gait disturbance, cognitive impairment and urinary incontinence, with gait usually appearing first and most disabling
Gait is shuffling, wide-based and magnetic with difficulty turning and impaired postural reflexes
Cognitive impairment is a subcortical pattern with slowed processing, attention and executive dysfunction rather than prominent early memory loss
No focal weakness, sensory loss, resting tremor, rigidity, papilledema or meningismus on exam
Ventriculomegaly out of proportion to cortical atrophy on imaging, often with an Evan's index greater than 0.3 and a DESH pattern (tight high-convexity sulci with widened Sylvian fissures)
CSF opening pressure is normal or high-normal with normal cell count, protein and glucose, excluding meningitis
Reversible causes such as hypothyroidism, vitamin B12 deficiency, depression and medication effects are excluded
A positive large-volume lumbar puncture (tap test) or external lumbar drainage trial supports shunt-responsive normal pressure hydrocephalus
Look-alikes such as Parkinson disease, Alzheimer disease, vascular dementia, Lewy body dementia, cervical spondylotic myelopathy and medication-induced parkinsonism are considered and distinguished

easy: Older adult with the full triad of magnetic gait, cognitive slowing and urinary incontinence
Gait difficulty clearly precedes the cognitive and bladder symptoms
MRI shows ventriculomegaly out of proportion to atrophy with a DESH pattern
Normal CSF opening pressure with normal cell count, protein and glucose
No resting tremor, rigidity or focal neurologic deficits
medium: Only one or two features of the triad are present at presentation
Symptoms attributed to normal aging or to coexisting vascular disease and polypharmacy
Coexisting hypertension, diabetes or prior stroke raises vascular dementia as a competing diagnosis
Mild cognitive impairment with relatively preserved gait early in the course
Tap test result is equivocal and an external lumbar drainage trial is needed
hard: Older adult with gait-predominant symptoms and minimal cognitive complaints, mimicking a gait disorder or myelopathy
Prominent urinary symptoms leading to a urologic workup before the neurologic cause is considered
Coexisting Parkinson disease or Alzheimer disease obscuring the underlying hydrocephalus
Ventriculomegaly proportionate to cortical atrophy, making imaging interpretation difficult
Rapidly progressive symptoms over days to weeks, suggesting an alternative cause such as tumor, abscess or rapidly progressive hydrocephalus
Patient on dopamine-blocking medications with parkinsonism that could explain the gait and cognitive findings
